evidence.note: tests/test_lane_launch_generic.py 21 tests pass (generic claude-shaped launch against fake_agent.py, level-1 conformance, descriptor gaps refuse naming the next call, opencode/kilo digest and extension unchanged); tests/test_lane_launch.py, test_lane_opencode.py, test_lane_driver.py pass; commits on ddflow/XA-lane-generic-prepare

chunk_findings.detail: `problems` accepts `autonomy`, `effort`, and `max_turns` for any launchable non-registered harness without checking that the harness descriptor actually supports those fields. The field comments and intent say these fields need descriptor support (`[headless].effort_flag`, `[headless].max_turns_flag`, an `[autonomy]` profile, etc.), and the intent explicitly says unknown fields should stay unavailable/refused. The code only rejects these fields when `_registered(t.harness)` is true. For example, given a project descriptor for `fake` that is launchable but has no `[headless].effort_flag`, `problems(Template(name="t", harness="fake", route="r", family="f", min_hooks="detect", budget_usd=1, effort="high"), root)` returns no problem because `launchable("fake", root)` is empty and `_registered("fake")` is false, even though `effort` is an unflagged/unknown launch field that should be refused before approval.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/launch_template.py:problems

chunk_findings.detail: `project_of` canonicalizes the path with `Path(path).resolve()` before searching for `.ddflow`, so it can miss or change the project root when symlinks are used. For example, if `/proj/.ddflow` is a symlink to `/shared/ddflow` (a directory not named `.ddflow`), loading `/proj/.ddflow/local/lane-templates.toml` resolves to `/shared/ddflow/local/lane-templates.toml`; none of its ancestors contains a `.ddflow` directory, so `load` gets `root=None`. The descriptor overrides under `/proj` are then not consulted, so a harness that should be launchable from that project's descriptor may be rejected. Conversely, if the symlink target lies under another project, validation uses the wrong project's descriptors. The docstring promises the nearest ancestor holding a `.ddflow` directory, and `/proj` holds one via the symlink.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/launch_template.py:project_of

chunk_findings.detail: `select_binary` accepts an `environ` mapping but uses it only to look up the `DDFLOW_<ID>_BIN` override; the actual PATH search is done by `shutil.which` with its default environment. Concrete failure: with `/tmp/bin/stub` executable, `os.environ["PATH"]` not containing `/tmp/bin`, and a call like `select_binary("stub", root, environ={"PATH": "/tmp/bin"})`, the function returns `unavailable` even though the supplied environment says the binary is on PATH. Any caller or test that tries to isolate PATH by passing a custom `environ` will get a false “not installed” result.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py `select_binary`

chunk_findings.detail: `descriptor` swallows `DescriptorError` and returns `None`, so `why_not` reports `no harness descriptor` even when a descriptor file exists but is malformed or rejected. Concrete failure: create `.ddflow/harnesses.d/foo.toml` with invalid TOML (or an error raised by `HR.load_in`); `why_not("foo", repo)` tells the user to add the descriptor instead of reporting that the existing override is invalid, sending them to the wrong fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py `descriptor` / `why_not`

chunk_findings.detail: The added help text says `lanes.stream_rules_dir` has default `.ddflow/streams.d/<harness>.toml`, while the new upgrade note for the same knob (`knob_added.lanes.stream_rules_dir.toml`) declares `new = '".ddflow/streams.d"'` and describes it as a project directory. If a user or agent follows the help and sets the knob to the documented default file path, e.g. `lanes.stream_rules_dir = ".ddflow/streams.d/claude.toml"`, the directory-based lookup implied by the knob will not find the harness stream rules as expected; the configured path is treated as a directory rather than the rules file, so stream rules can be silently ignored. The docs should say the default directory is `.ddflow/streams.d`, with `<harness>.toml` resolved inside it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/prompts/help/lanes.md:Launching a lane of any harness

chunk_findings.detail: The new section states “a descriptor with `[headless]` is launchable,” but the same section later says a descriptor with no autonomy profile refuses and that for MCP “No flag, no launch” unless `[headless].mcp_flag` or a `{mcp_config}` argv element is present. Given a project override descriptor that has `[headless].argv` but no autonomy profile or MCP flag, the headline guidance says it is launchable while the described behavior refuses to launch; this can cause an operator to add a minimal `[headless]` block and expect `lanes.launch` to start it.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/lane-driver.md:97

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to verify that the fake agent sees the prompt on stdin, but it never observes stdin. The wrapper records only argv and selected environment variables, and the assertions only check that the stream rules map the recording to `started`/`usage` events and that `usage` is in the handle capabilities. If generic prepare stops writing the approved prompt to the child process’s stdin (for example, passing it only as a file path or omitting it), the fake agent can still emit `RECORDING` and this test still passes, so it cannot detect the stdin-delivery regression it says it covers.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lane_launch_generic.py:test_the_fake_agent_sees_the_prompt_on_stdin_and_the_stream_maps_to_events

chunk_findings.detail: When `ext.prepare()` returns `LH.Consent`, `_prepare` calls `ext.cleanup(req.home)` before returning the refusal. The consent flow is explicitly described as asking for consent in the lane’s private home, so removing that home deletes the consent artifacts the operator needs to inspect/approve. A template whose harness uses a hook plugin that has not yet been consented will therefore produce a refusal whose `Consent.how` refers to a now-deleted home; the approval step cannot be completed, and repeated launches recreate and immediately delete the consent, preventing the lane from ever passing consent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/launch.py:_prepare

chunk_findings.detail: For descriptor-driven harnesses, `problems` does not validate template launch fields against the descriptor’s flags. `launchable`/`prepare.why_not` take only the harness name, and the template-aware check is guarded by `_registered(t.harness)`. Given a non-registered harness `foo` whose descriptor has `[headless]` but no `effort_flag` or `max_turns_flag`, a template such as `Template(name="foo", harness="foo", route="r", family="f", budget_usd=1, effort="high", max_turns=5)` returns no error from `problems`: `launchable("foo", root)` is `""`, `_generic_only(t)` is non-empty, but `_registered("foo")` is false, so the check is skipped. The field comments and the change intent require those fields to be unavailable unless the descriptor declares the corresponding flag, so this invalid template passes preflight/approval and can then fail late or launch without the requested limits.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/launch_template.py:problems

chunk_findings.detail: `load` now calls `project_of(path)` before the `if not path.is_file(): return {}, []` guard. `project_of` starts with `Path(path).resolve()`, which raises `OSError`/`RuntimeError` for a path containing a symlink loop, while `path.is_file()` would have returned `False` and the function would have returned no templates and no note. For example, if `lane-templates.toml` is a symlink to itself, `load(Path("lane-templates.toml"))` previously returned `({}, [])`, but with this change it crashes during `resolve()` instead of treating the unavailable file as no templates.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/launch_template.py:load

chunk_findings.detail: `select_binary` accepts an `environ` mapping but only uses it to read the `DDFLOW_<ID>_BIN` override; the PATH searches call `shutil.which(command)` and `shutil.which(command, path=dirs)`, which consult the real process environment, not the supplied mapping. Given `select_binary("foo", environ={"PATH": "/custom", "DDFLOW_FOO_BIN": ""})` with `/custom/foo` executable but `foo` absent from the real PATH, the function returns `unavailable`; conversely, `environ={"PATH": ""}` can still find and launch a `foo` binary from the real PATH, defeating the caller’s environment isolation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py:select_binary

chunk_findings.detail: The module’s own `_ID` grammar permits harness ids containing `-`, but the binary override name is built by `OC.ENV_PATTERN.format(harness.upper())` without converting `-` to `_`. For a descriptor id `my-harness`, the generated override variable name contains a hyphen (e.g. `DDFLOW_MY-HARNESS_BIN`), which is not a usable POSIX shell environment variable; a user setting the conventional `DDFLOW_MY_HARNESS_BIN` will have it ignored, and `select_binary` returns `unavailable` when the harness is not already on PATH.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py:select_binary

chunk_findings.detail: `descriptor` catches `DescriptorError` and returns `None`, so `why_not` reports a missing descriptor for an existing but invalid one. Given a malformed `.ddflow/harnesses.d/foo.toml` (for example invalid TOML), `why_not("foo")` returns “no harness descriptor for ‘foo’: add …” instead of the parse error; if a shipped `foo` descriptor also exists, it is discarded too, so a valid launch is blocked with a misleading message.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py:descriptor

chunk_findings.detail: The help text says `lanes.stream_rules_dir` defaults to `.ddflow/streams.d/<harness>.toml`, while the new upgrade note defines the same knob as a directory default `.ddflow/streams.d` containing one `<harness>.toml` per harness. If a user follows the help and sets `lanes.stream_rules_dir = ".ddflow/streams.d/claude.toml"`, the knob’s stated directory semantics mean the launch will treat that file path as a directory and fail to find the per-harness rules file inside it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/prompts/help/lanes.md:55

chunk_findings.detail: The section says “a descriptor with `[headless]` is launchable,” but later in the same section it says “a descriptor with no autonomy profile … refuses.” That is directly contradictory: a project override such as `.ddflow/harnesses.d/foo.toml` containing `[headless]` but no `[autonomy]` profile is documented as launchable by the first sentence, yet cannot launch according to the second. The docs should say that `[headless]` is necessary but not sufficient, or list the required descriptor fields, so users do not add a `[headless]` block and expect `lanes.launch` to work.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/lane-driver.md:97

chunk_findings.detail: The generated fake binary embeds `sys.executable` directly in a POSIX shebang (`#!{py}`). If the test interpreter path contains spaces (e.g. a virtualenv at `/tmp/my venv/bin/python`) or is longer than the kernel shebang limit, executing `tmp_path/bin/claude` fails before Python starts: the kernel splits the shebang on spaces and tries to run `/tmp/my`, so `LN.launch` cannot start the fake agent and the launch tests fail. The `os.execv` call inside the script would handle a spaced `sys.executable`, but the shebang line does not.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lane_launch_generic.py `WRAPPER` / `fake_claude`

chunk_findings.detail: This is the only successful-launch test that does not call `r.release()`. It launches a lane, consumes events, calls `r.driver.stop(...)`, and then calls `PR.resolve("claude", repo).cleanup(home)`. Given this test’s input, the lane lease/registration that `Launched.release()` is responsible for is left unreleased while the lane home is removed, leaking lane state and potentially causing stale-lane or finalizer problems in the suite; the other successful launch tests release before cleanup.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_lane_launch_generic.py `test_the_fake_agent_sees_the_prompt_on_stdin_and_the_stream_maps_to_events`

If a caller passes `environ={"PATH": ""}` while the process `os.environ["PATH"]` contains the descriptor command, `path = environ.get("PATH")` is `""`, so the changed expression falls through to `which(command)` with the default environment and can return an executable path. `select_binary` then reports the binary as available even though the caller-supplied environment has no search path; it should honour an empty PATH (e.g. call `which(command, path=path)` whenever `path is not None`) rather than falling back to the process environment.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py:select_binary

chunk_findings.detail: When `ext.prepare()` returns `LH.Consent`, `_prepare` calls `ext.cleanup(req.home)` before returning the refusal. The consent flow is explicitly described as asking for consent in the lane’s private home, so removing that home deletes the consent artifacts the operator needs to inspect/approve. A template whose harness uses a hook plugin that has not yet been consented will therefore produce a refusal whose `Consent.how` refers to a now-deleted home; the approval step cannot be completed, and repeated launches recreate and immediately delete the consent, preventing the lane from ever passing consent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/launch.py:_prepare

chunk_findings.detail: For descriptor-driven harnesses, `problems` does not validate template launch fields against the descriptor’s flags. `launchable`/`prepare.why_not` take only the harness name, and the template-aware check is guarded by `_registered(t.harness)`. Given a non-registered harness `foo` whose descriptor has `[headless]` but no `effort_flag` or `max_turns_flag`, a template such as `Template(name="foo", harness="foo", route="r", family="f", budget_usd=1, effort="high", max_turns=5)` returns no error from `problems`: `launchable("foo", root)` is `""`, `_generic_only(t)` is non-empty, but `_registered("foo")` is false, so the check is skipped. The field comments and the change intent require those fields to be unavailable unless the descriptor declares the corresponding flag, so this invalid template passes preflight/approval and can then fail late or launch without the requested limits.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/launch_template.py:problems

chunk_findings.detail: `load` now calls `project_of(path)` before the `if not path.is_file(): return {}, []` guard. `project_of` starts with `Path(path).resolve()`, which raises `OSError`/`RuntimeError` for a path containing a symlink loop, while `path.is_file()` would have returned `False` and the function would have returned no templates and no note. For example, if `lane-templates.toml` is a symlink to itself, `load(Path("lane-templates.toml"))` previously returned `({}, [])`, but with this change it crashes during `resolve()` instead of treating the unavailable file as no templates.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/launch_template.py:load

chunk_findings.detail: `select_binary` accepts an `environ` mapping but only uses it to read the `DDFLOW_<ID>_BIN` override; the PATH searches call `shutil.which(command)` and `shutil.which(command, path=dirs)`, which consult the real process environment, not the supplied mapping. Given `select_binary("foo", environ={"PATH": "/custom", "DDFLOW_FOO_BIN": ""})` with `/custom/foo` executable but `foo` absent from the real PATH, the function returns `unavailable`; conversely, `environ={"PATH": ""}` can still find and launch a `foo` binary from the real PATH, defeating the caller’s environment isolation.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py:select_binary

chunk_findings.detail: The module’s own `_ID` grammar permits harness ids containing `-`, but the binary override name is built by `OC.ENV_PATTERN.format(harness.upper())` without converting `-` to `_`. For a descriptor id `my-harness`, the generated override variable name contains a hyphen (e.g. `DDFLOW_MY-HARNESS_BIN`), which is not a usable POSIX shell environment variable; a user setting the conventional `DDFLOW_MY_HARNESS_BIN` will have it ignored, and `select_binary` returns `unavailable` when the harness is not already on PATH.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py:select_binary

chunk_findings.detail: `descriptor` catches `DescriptorError` and returns `None`, so `why_not` reports a missing descriptor for an existing but invalid one. Given a malformed `.ddflow/harnesses.d/foo.toml` (for example invalid TOML), `why_not("foo")` returns “no harness descriptor for ‘foo’: add …” instead of the parse error; if a shipped `foo` descriptor also exists, it is discarded too, so a valid launch is blocked with a misleading message.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py:descriptor

chunk_findings.detail: The help text says `lanes.stream_rules_dir` defaults to `.ddflow/streams.d/<harness>.toml`, while the new upgrade note defines the same knob as a directory default `.ddflow/streams.d` containing one `<harness>.toml` per harness. If a user follows the help and sets `lanes.stream_rules_dir = ".ddflow/streams.d/claude.toml"`, the knob’s stated directory semantics mean the launch will treat that file path as a directory and fail to find the per-harness rules file inside it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/prompts/help/lanes.md:55

chunk_findings.detail: The section says “a descriptor with `[headless]` is launchable,” but later in the same section it says “a descriptor with no autonomy profile … refuses.” That is directly contradictory: a project override such as `.ddflow/harnesses.d/foo.toml` containing `[headless]` but no `[autonomy]` profile is documented as launchable by the first sentence, yet cannot launch according to the second. The docs should say that `[headless]` is necessary but not sufficient, or list the required descriptor fields, so users do not add a `[headless]` block and expect `lanes.launch` to work.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/lane-driver.md:97

chunk_findings.detail: The generated fake binary embeds `sys.executable` directly in a POSIX shebang (`#!{py}`). If the test interpreter path contains spaces (e.g. a virtualenv at `/tmp/my venv/bin/python`) or is longer than the kernel shebang limit, executing `tmp_path/bin/claude` fails before Python starts: the kernel splits the shebang on spaces and tries to run `/tmp/my`, so `LN.launch` cannot start the fake agent and the launch tests fail. The `os.execv` call inside the script would handle a spaced `sys.executable`, but the shebang line does not.

chunk_findings.detail: This is the only successful-launch test that does not call `r.release()`. It launches a lane, consumes events, calls `r.driver.stop(...)`, and then calls `PR.resolve("claude", repo).cleanup(home)`. Given this test’s input, the lane lease/registration that `Launched.release()` is responsible for is left unreleased while the lane home is removed, leaking lane state and potentially causing stale-lane or finalizer problems in the suite; the other successful launch tests release before cleanup.

chunk_findings.detail: For a harness that is both registered (e.g. `opencode`) and has a descriptor capable of honouring a generic launch field, `_harness_problems` still refuses the template solely because of the `_registered` constant guard. Given a template with `harness="opencode"` and a field included in `_generic_only(t)` such as `effort="high"`, plus a project descriptor `.ddflow/harnesses.d/opencode.toml` containing a complete `[headless]`, `[detect]`, and `[autonomy]` record and `[headless] effort_flag = "--effort"`, `launchable("opencode", root)` returns no reason. `_harness_problems` then returns `effort not supported by harness 'opencode's launch` without calling `prepare.template_gaps`, even though the descriptor explicitly says the launch can honour `effort`. This blocks descriptor-driven launch for registered harnesses and contradicts the stated intent that a descriptor with `[headless]` is launchable and that the special-case path is not the only path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/launch_template.py:_harness_problems

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding 4 was triaged as fixed, but the fix still consults the real process environment when the supplied `environ` explicitly contains an empty `PATH`. The new search line `or (which(command, path=path) if path else which(command))` treats `path == ""` as false and calls `which(command)`, which uses `os.environ["PATH"]`, not the caller-supplied mapping. Given `select_binary("foo", root, environ={"PATH": "", "DDFLOW_FOO_BIN": ""})` where `foo` is executable somewhere on the real process `PATH` but not in the current directory, the function can return an available binary even though the supplied environment contains no PATH entries. This defeats the purpose of the injected `environ` mapping and can make tests or restricted launch paths incorrectly report that a harness binary is available.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py:select_binary

chunk_findings.detail: `problems` accepts `autonomy`, `effort`, and `max_turns` for any launchable non-registered harness without checking that the harness descriptor actually supports those fields. The field comments and intent say these fields need descriptor support (`[headless].effort_flag`, `[headless].max_turns_flag`, an `[autonomy]` profile, etc.), and the intent explicitly says unknown fields should stay unavailable/refused. The code only rejects these fields when `_registered(t.harness)` is true. For example, given a project descriptor for `fake` that is launchable but has no `[headless].effort_flag`, `problems(Template(name="t", harness="fake", route="r", family="f", min_hooks="detect", budget_usd=1, effort="high"), root)` returns no problem because `launchable("fake", root)` is empty and `_registered("fake")` is false, even though `effort` is an unflagged/unknown launch field that should be refused before approval.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/launch_template.py:problems

chunk_findings.detail: `project_of` canonicalizes the path with `Path(path).resolve()` before searching for `.ddflow`, so it can miss or change the project root when symlinks are used. For example, if `/proj/.ddflow` is a symlink to `/shared/ddflow` (a directory not named `.ddflow`), loading `/proj/.ddflow/local/lane-templates.toml` resolves to `/shared/ddflow/local/lane-templates.toml`; none of its ancestors contains a `.ddflow` directory, so `load` gets `root=None`. The descriptor overrides under `/proj` are then not consulted, so a harness that should be launchable from that project's descriptor may be rejected. Conversely, if the symlink target lies under another project, validation uses the wrong project's descriptors. The docstring promises the nearest ancestor holding a `.ddflow` directory, and `/proj` holds one via the symlink.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/launch_template.py:project_of

chunk_findings.detail: `select_binary` accepts an `environ` mapping but uses it only to look up the `DDFLOW_<ID>_BIN` override; the actual PATH search is done by `shutil.which` with its default environment. Concrete failure: with `/tmp/bin/stub` executable, `os.environ["PATH"]` not containing `/tmp/bin`, and a call like `select_binary("stub", root, environ={"PATH": "/tmp/bin"})`, the function returns `unavailable` even though the supplied environment says the binary is on PATH. Any caller or test that tries to isolate PATH by passing a custom `environ` will get a false “not installed” result.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py `select_binary`

chunk_findings.detail: `descriptor` swallows `DescriptorError` and returns `None`, so `why_not` reports `no harness descriptor` even when a descriptor file exists but is malformed or rejected. Concrete failure: create `.ddflow/harnesses.d/foo.toml` with invalid TOML (or an error raised by `HR.load_in`); `why_not("foo", repo)` tells the user to add the descriptor instead of reporting that the existing override is invalid, sending them to the wrong fix.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/lanes/prepare.py `descriptor` / `why_not`

chunk_findings.detail: The added help text says `lanes.stream_rules_dir` has default `.ddflow/streams.d/<harness>.toml`, while the new upgrade note for the same knob (`knob_added.lanes.stream_rules_dir.toml`) declares `new = '".ddflow/streams.d"'` and describes it as a project directory. If a user or agent follows the help and sets the knob to the documented default file path, e.g. `lanes.stream_rules_dir = ".ddflow/streams.d/claude.toml"`, the directory-based lookup implied by the knob will not find the harness stream rules as expected; the configured path is treated as a directory rather than the rules file, so stream rules can be silently ignored. The docs should say the default directory is `.ddflow/streams.d`, with `<harness>.toml` resolved inside it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/templates/prompts/help/lanes.md:Launching a lane of any harness

chunk_findings.detail: The new section states “a descriptor with `[headless]` is launchable,” but the same section later says a descriptor with no autonomy profile refuses and that for MCP “No flag, no launch” unless `[headless].mcp_flag` or a `{mcp_config}` argv element is present. Given a project override descriptor that has `[headless].argv` but no autonomy profile or MCP flag, the headline guidance says it is launchable while the described behavior refuses to launch; this can cause an operator to add a minimal `[headless]` block and expect `lanes.launch` to start it.
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/lane-driver.md:97

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to verify that the fake agent sees the prompt on stdin, but it never observes stdin. The wrapper records only argv and selected environment variables, and the assertions only check that the stream rules map the recording to `started`/`usage` events and that `usage` is in the handle capabilities. If generic prepare stops writing the approved prompt to the child process’s stdin (for example, passing it only as a file path or omitting it), the fake agent can still emit `RECORDING` and this test still passes, so it cannot detect the stdin-delivery regression it says it covers.
